title: The Functions of Body Systems
description: How the skeletal, muscular, cardiovascular and respiratory systems work together to support sport and exercise.
content_html:
Why Functions Matter

Understanding how each body system works is the foundation of sport science. Coaches, physiotherapists and athletes all need to know what each system does — not just what it is made of — so they can explain why performance improves with training, or why it breaks down with fatigue. This lesson examines the four key systems: skeletal, muscular, cardiovascular and respiratory, and explores the specific jobs each one carries out during sport and exercise.

Functions of the Skeletal System

The skeletal system performs six important functions. First, it provides support — the vertebral column and leg bones act as a structural framework that holds the body upright against gravity, which is essential for every sporting activity from swimming to weightlifting. Second, it offers protection to vital organs: the cranium shields the brain, the ribcage guards the heart and lungs, and the vertebral column protects the spinal cord. Third, bones create movement through levers — they act as rigid levers that muscles pull on to generate movement at synovial joints. Every time a sprinter drives their leg backward or a tennis player swings their racket, a lever system is at work.

Fourth, the skeleton provides the body with its structural shape — the characteristic human silhouette is determined by bone structure, and this shape influences posture and aerodynamic efficiency in sport. Fifth, certain bones — particularly the long bones such as the femur and humerus, and flat bones such as the sternum — contain red bone marrow that carries out blood cell production. Red blood cells manufactured here carry oxygen to working muscles, making this function directly relevant to aerobic performance. Sixth, bones act as a mineral store, holding approximately 99% of the body's calcium and significant amounts of phosphorus. These minerals are released into the bloodstream when needed and are also essential for normal muscle contraction.

Key Fact

The six functions of the skeletal system are: support, protection, movement through levers, structural shape, blood-cell production in red bone marrow, and mineral storage (especially calcium and phosphorus). All six may be tested in short-answer questions.

Functions of the Muscular System

The muscular system's primary function is to produce movement through contraction. Muscles can only pull — they cannot push — so they are arranged in antagonistic pairs. At the elbow, the biceps acts as the agonist during flexion, shortening to bend the arm, while the triceps acts as the antagonist and relaxes to allow the movement. During extension — for example, a basketball chest pass — the roles reverse. The specification requires knowledge of antagonistic action at both the elbow and the knee (quadriceps and hamstrings). Muscles also have synergist muscles that assist the agonist, and fixator muscles that stabilise the joint to allow efficient movement.

Beyond movement, the muscular system maintains posture — deep postural muscles such as the abdominals, erector spinae and trapezius are in a state of continuous partial contraction to hold the body in alignment during both rest and activity. Good posture reduces injury risk and improves mechanical efficiency in sport. The muscular system also plays a major role in generating heat. Muscle contractions are only about 25% mechanically efficient — the remaining 75% of the energy released is lost as heat. This thermogenic function helps the body maintain its core temperature during exercise in cold environments, which is why vigorous activity warms you up rapidly.

Key Fact

Muscular system functions: movement via contraction (agonist/antagonist pairs), maintaining posture through continuous partial contraction, and generating heat as a by-product of muscle metabolism. At the knee, quadriceps = agonist for extension; hamstrings = agonist for flexion.

Functions of the Cardiovascular System

The cardiovascular system (the systemic or pulmonary circulatory system) has three core functions. Its primary role is the transport of oxygen and nutrients to working muscles and organs. During exercise, cardiac output increases — the heart beats faster and pumps more blood per beat (stroke volume) — so that oxygen and glucose reach the muscles rapidly enough to sustain contraction. Without this delivery, muscles would switch to anaerobic metabolism and fatigue rapidly.

The second function is the removal of waste products, including carbon dioxide and lactic acid produced during exercise. Deoxygenated blood carrying CO2 returns via the veins to the right side of the heart, from where it is pumped to the lungs (the pulmonary circuit) to release CO2 and collect fresh oxygen. Lactic acid is transported to the liver for conversion. The third function is regulation of body temperature. When the body overheats during exercise, vasodilation occurs — blood vessels near the skin surface widen, bringing warm blood to the surface where heat can be lost to the environment. When the body is cold, vasoconstriction narrows these vessels to retain core heat. This temperature-regulation mechanism is directly assessable in the written examination.

Vasodilation is the widening of blood vessels — particularly those supplying the skin — which allows more warm blood to reach the surface so that heat can radiate away from the body into the environment. This is why the skin looks flushed and red during or after vigorous exercise. Vasoconstriction is the opposite: blood vessels narrow, restricting blood flow to the skin and extremities so that warm blood is redirected to the vital organs and working muscles, conserving core temperature in cold conditions or at rest. Both processes are controlled by the autonomic nervous system and happen automatically in response to changes in core and ambient temperature. Understanding this mechanism is essential for explaining why a long-distance runner may feel warm even in cold weather.

Functions of the Respiratory System

The respiratory system drives breathing — the mechanical process of moving air in and out of the lungs. During inspiration (breathing in), the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the intercostal muscles between the ribs contract to lift the ribcage outward and upward, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity. This reduces internal air pressure below atmospheric pressure, so air rushes into the lungs. During expiration (breathing out), the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, the ribcage drops inward and downward, volume decreases, pressure rises and air is forced out. At rest this happens around 12-20 times per minute; during intense exercise breathing rate can exceed 40-50 breaths per minute.

The second and most critical function is gaseous exchange at the alveoli. The alveoli are surrounded by a dense network of capillaries. Oxygen diffuses from the high concentration inside the alveoli across the thin alveolar wall into the blood (where oxygen concentration is lower), binding to haemoglobin in red blood cells. At the same time, carbon dioxide — in high concentration in the blood after being produced by working muscles — diffuses in the opposite direction, from the blood into the alveoli, and is then expelled during expiration. This process of diffusion is passive and depends on the concentration gradient being maintained: the continuous flow of blood removes oxygenated blood and brings fresh deoxygenated blood, keeping the gradient steep and exchange efficient.

The cardiovascular and respiratory systems are inseparable partners — together they form the cardiorespiratory system. The respiratory system gets oxygen into the blood and removes carbon dioxide at the alveoli; the cardiovascular system then transports that oxygenated blood to the muscles and returns deoxygenated blood back to the lungs. During exercise, both systems respond simultaneously: breathing rate and depth increase to bring more oxygen to the alveoli, while heart rate and stroke volume increase to deliver more oxygenated blood to the working muscles. If either system fails to keep up — for example, if breathing rate cannot rise quickly enough — performance drops and the athlete enters anaerobic metabolism more quickly. Exam questions often require you to link both systems when explaining why performance changes with exercise intensity.
exam_tip_html: Extended-answer questions often ask you to describe or explain the functions of a named body system in a sporting context — for example, "explain how the cardiovascular system supports a marathon runner". Structure your answer by naming each function, explaining the mechanism, and linking it to the sporting scenario. For the respiratory system, be precise: gaseous exchange occurs at the alveoli by diffusion (not osmosis). For the muscular system, always name the agonist and antagonist at the specific joint the question asks about — a generic answer about "muscles contracting" will not score full marks. For 6-mark or 8-mark questions, try to link two or more systems together to demonstrate how they work in combination during sport.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The skeletal system has six functions: support, protection, movement through levers, structural shape, blood-cell production and mineral storage. All six can be examined individually.
  • The muscular system produces movement via antagonistic pairs (agonist contracts, antagonist relaxes), maintains posture through continuous partial contraction, and generates heat as a by-product of metabolism.
  • The cardiovascular system transports oxygen and nutrients to working muscles, removes waste products (CO2, lactic acid), and regulates body temperature through vasodilation and vasoconstriction.
  • The respiratory system drives breathing via the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, and enables gaseous exchange at the alveoli — oxygen diffuses into the blood, carbon dioxide diffuses out.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a function of the skeletal system?
A) Gaseous exchange
B) Blood-cell production
C) Vasodilation
D) Antagonistic action
State two functions of the muscular system during sport and exercise.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct functions from: movement through contraction / agonist-antagonist action; maintaining posture; generating heat. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the cardiovascular system regulates body temperature during vigorous exercise.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'blood vessels widen'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'vasodilation causes blood vessels near the skin surface to widen, bringing warm blood to the surface where heat is lost to the environment'). A third mark is awarded for also mentioning vasoconstriction as the opposing mechanism used when the body needs to retain heat, or for explaining the role of the autonomic nervous system in controlling both processes. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of gaseous exchange that occurs in the respiratory system during exercise.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the alveoli as the site of exchange (1); oxygen diffuses from alveoli into the blood (capillaries) due to a concentration gradient (1); carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction, from the blood into the alveoli (1); CO2 is then expelled during expiration while oxygenated blood is transported to working muscles by the cardiovascular system (1). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A football player is sprinting at high intensity during the second half of a match. Using your knowledge of two body systems, explain how the body responds to meet the increased demand for oxygen in the working muscles.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Detailed explanation of both the cardiovascular system (heart rate and stroke volume increase to raise cardiac output; more oxygenated blood delivered per minute; vasodilation redirects blood to working muscles) and the respiratory system (breathing rate and tidal volume increase; more oxygen reaches alveoli; gaseous exchange rate increases via diffusion). Clear link between both systems and the specific demand of the scenario.
Secure (3-4 marks): Both systems identified with reasonable explanation but limited application to the sprint scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One system explained, or both identified without explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
During a bicep curl exercise, identify the agonist and antagonist muscles acting at the elbow joint during the upward phase. Explain the antagonistic action taking place and describe one other function of the muscular system that occurs during this movement.

A weightlifter is lifting a heavy barbell overhead in a cold gym. Discuss how two body systems respond to support this performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Part 1 — biceps = agonist (contracts to flex the elbow, pulling the forearm upward); triceps = antagonist (relaxes to allow the movement). Antagonistic action explained clearly (agonist shortens, antagonist lengthens). Second muscular function: e.g. fixator muscles stabilise the shoulder joint; core muscles maintain posture; heat is generated as a by-product of contraction (any one with brief explanation). Part 2 — musculoskeletal: bones act as levers at the shoulder, elbow and wrist joints, with muscles attached via tendons pulling on these levers to create upward movement; skeletal function of protection (ribcage/spine under load). Cardiovascular: vasoconstriction in a cold environment to retain heat; increased cardiac output to deliver oxygen and nutrients to working muscles. Both systems applied to the weightlifting context with a substantiated judgement about which system is most critical.
Secure (5-6 marks): Agonist/antagonist correctly identified, second function noted, two systems explained with reasonable application.
Developing (3-4 marks): Partial credit on antagonistic action, one system explained.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, limited development. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which function of the skeletal system involves red bone marrow producing red blood cells that carry oxygen to working muscles?
During vasodilation, blood vessels near the skin surface widen so that warm blood reaches the surface and heat can be lost to the environment. This is a function of which body system?
The muscle that contracts to produce the desired movement at a joint is called the _____; the muscle on the opposing side that relaxes to allow that movement is the antagonist.
Gaseous exchange at the _____ involves oxygen diffusing into the blood and carbon dioxide diffusing out, driven by concentration gradients.
Match each body system to one of its key functions.
right: Maintains posture through continuous partial contraction of postural muscles
Drives gaseous exchange at the alveoli — oxygen in, carbon dioxide out
Stores minerals such as calcium and phosphorus in bone tissue

flashcard_questions.q: What are the six functions of the skeletal system?
flashcard_questions.a: Support, protection, movement through levers, structural shape, blood-cell production, mineral storage.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the skeletal system use to produce red blood cells?
flashcard_questions.a: Red bone marrow found in long and flat bones.

flashcard_questions.q: Which minerals does the skeletal system store?
flashcard_questions.a: Primarily calcium and phosphorus, essential for muscle contraction and bone strength.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an antagonistic pair of muscles?
flashcard_questions.a: Two muscles working in opposition — the agonist contracts while the antagonist relaxes.

flashcard_questions.q: At the elbow during flexion, which muscle is the agonist and which is the antagonist?
Why does the muscular system generate heat during exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Muscle contractions are only about 25% efficient; the remaining energy is released as heat.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three functions of the cardiovascular system?
flashcard_questions.a: Transporting oxygen and nutrients, removing waste products, and regulating body temperature.

flashcard_questions.q: What is vasodilation and when does it occur?
flashcard_questions.a: Widening of blood vessels near the skin surface to lose heat — occurs during vigorous exercise.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of the diaphragm during inspiration?
flashcard_questions.a: It contracts and flattens to increase chest volume, drawing air into the lungs.

flashcard_questions.q: Where does gaseous exchange take place in the respiratory system?
flashcard_questions.a: At the alveoli — tiny air sacs surrounded by capillaries in the lungs.

flashcard_questions.q: Which direction does oxygen move during gaseous exchange, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: From alveoli into the blood, because oxygen concentration is higher in the alveoli.

flashcard_questions.q: How do the cardiovascular and respiratory systems work together during exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Respiration loads oxygen into the blood at the alveoli; the cardiovascular system delivers it to muscles.

glossary_terms.definition: The framework of bones that gives the body its shape and protects vital organs, enables movement through levers, produces blood cells and stores minerals.
Pairs of muscles that work in opposition: as one muscle (the agonist) contracts to produce movement, the opposing muscle (the antagonist) relaxes to allow that movement.
The prime mover — the muscle that contracts to produce the desired movement at a joint.
The heart and blood vessels that form the systemic circulatory system, transporting oxygen, nutrients and hormones around the body while removing waste products.
Tiny air sacs at the end of the bronchioles in the lungs where gaseous exchange takes place — oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out.
